_meta.method: The physical chain, with the OBSERVED value that shows each link is currently active. MOSTLY observation, not entirely: rows carry a status, and one cascade step (the delayed onset of the southern-African rains) is a published FEWS NET FORECAST, marked as such. The sources list includes IRI's QuickLook, which is a forecast product. Every number is something an agency has published and dated; where that agency was predicting rather than measuring, the row says so.
_meta.why: The panel could say what El Niño does to 35 countries without ever saying what El Niño IS. A reader who does not know that the trade winds have reversed cannot judge whether any of the rest is plausible. This is the mechanism, stated once, with its evidence.
_meta.canonical_form: Follows the three-panel convention used by NOAA PMEL's TAO schematic, NOAA Climate.gov's Walker circulation figure and the Bureau of Meteorology diagram that IRI republishes: neutral, El Nino and La Nina drawn to one scale, with the atmospheric circulation closed rather than shown as surface winds alone.

chain.title: The trade winds give way
chain.normal: Easterly trades blow along the equator, dragging surface water west and piling a warm pool against Indonesia. Sea level near Indonesia sits roughly half a metre higher than off Ecuador.
chain.now: Westerly anomalies at 850 hPa run from the western to the east-central Pacific and have persisted since mid-March 2026. BoM records the trades as "either reversed or weaker than average across the western tropical Pacific".
chain.evidence: 850-hPa westerly anomalies, 8 Jul – 6 Aug (IRI, 19 Aug 2026); CPC confirms them from mid-March 2026 (weekly update, 31 Aug 2026), and its 10 Sep 2026 discussion still has low-level westerly anomalies from the western to the east-central equatorial Pacific.

chain.title: The pressure see-saw tips
chain.normal: High pressure over the eastern Pacific, low over Indonesia. The gradient is what drives the trades. The Southern Oscillation Index measures it.
chain.now: The SOI is about two standard deviations negative. The July Troup SOI came in at −29.1, the most negative July in the record. BoM's 30-day Troup SOI stood at −18.7 on 14 September 2026, still far past the −7 that BoM treats as the El Niño side.
chain.evidence: July 2026 Troup SOI −29.1, most negative July on record. Consistent with CPC, BoM and JMA. BoM 30-day SOI −18.7 for the 30 days to 14 Sep 2026 (soi.txt).

chain.title: The warm pool slides east
chain.normal: Cold water upwells off South America; the thermocline sits shallow in the east and deep in the west.
chain.now: The thermocline is deeper than average across the eastern basin and the subsurface is extraordinarily warm. BoM calls the July equatorial upper-ocean heat anomaly the highest for any month since records began in 1979.
chain.evidence: CPC, 10 Sep 2026, verbatim: "Subsurface temperatures continued to be significantly above average, with widespread anomalies in excess of +10.0°C at depth." CPC's subsurface index, the 180°–100°W average, held steady through August; the +10 °C is the anomaly at depth, not a basin mean. IRI puts 50–150 m between 150°W and 80°W more than 8 °C above climatology in places.

chain.title: The rain moves with the warm water
chain.normal: Deep convection sits over the Maritime Continent, Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea. That is where the rain falls.
chain.now: Convection is enhanced along the equator from near the Date Line to the eastern Pacific, and suppressed over the Philippines, Indonesia and Papua New Guinea. The rain has moved with the warm water, and this is the single step that turns an ocean anomaly into a harvest problem.
chain.evidence: Below-average OLR from the Date Line eastward; above-average OLR over the Maritime Continent (CPC weekly, 31 Aug 2026). CPC's 10 Sep 2026 discussion: enhanced convection and rainfall persisted from the central to the eastern Pacific while remaining suppressed over Indonesia. BoM and JMA describe the same pattern independently.

chain.title: The Humboldt upwelling is capped
chain.normal: Cold, nutrient-rich water rises off Peru and feeds the largest single-species fishery on earth.
chain.now: The same warm layer that deepens the thermocline sits directly against the South American coast, capping the upwelling that the anchoveta depend on.
chain.evidence: Niño 1+2 at +4.5 °C (week of 9 Sep 2026): warm water hard against the coast, not only in the central basin. The August monthly mean was +3.4 °C (CPC, 10 Sep 2026).

flavour.title: This one is east-based, and that changes who it reaches
flavour.explainer: El Niño is not one pattern. The warming can sit in the central Pacific or hard against South America, and the two send their consequences to different places. This event is strongly east-based: the anomaly grows steadily from west to east across the four Niño regions.
flavour.sharpens: An east-based event maximises the coastal-Peru channel: flooding, huaicos and the anchoveta collapse. That is the best-quantified ENSO impact anywhere, with a clean chain from sea temperature to catch quota to fishmeal price. It resembles 1982-83 and 1997-98 more than the central-Pacific 2015-16 event.
flavour.blurs: It does not follow that everything is worse. The Indian monsoon and the western North Pacific typhoon season key partly off central Pacific warming, so an east-based event is not automatically the worse case for Asia.
flavour.open_gap: No expert was found making an on-the-record claim that this event's east-based structure will change its teleconnection footprint. The east-versus-central difference in Philippine landfalls in particular is unquantified. Treat the flavour as a reason to watch Peru closely and as an open question everywhere else.

sources.label: Peru ENFEN uses the ICEN over Niño 1+2, not the ONI, the two indices decouple

cascade.what: Trades reversed, SOI at a record-negative July, subsurface +10 °C, convection displaced east.
cascade.note: Every agency agrees on the phase. This is not only a sea-surface signal. The atmosphere is coupled, so teleconnections should be treated as live.

cascade.what: Delayed onset of the rains in northern Zambia, Malawi, northern Mozambique and Angola; suppressed convection over Indonesia and the Philippines.
cascade.note: FEWS NET explicitly forecasts a delayed onset. This is the first measurable consequence, and it is measurable in October, before any crop signal exists.

cascade.what: Farmers respond before the weather does. Planting intentions, area sown, and abandonment move first.
cascade.note: Where ENSO works through area sown rather than yield, as with Indonesian and Philippine rice, this panel's own yield model is blind by construction.

cascade.what: Southern African maize grain-fill in Feb–Mar, harvest May–Jul. Argentine maize and soy through NDJ and JFM. US winter wheat Jun–Aug, where El Niño tends to help. Australian wheat moves with the Indian Ocean Dipole as much as with El Niño.
cascade.note: The lag is the reason a strong August tells you nothing yet. Southern Africa is pre-plant right now: seed, fertiliser and credit decisions only. Nothing sown, nothing measurable.

cascade.what: Canal and river draft restrictions; domestic staple prices in deficit markets.
cascade.note: Already visible: Panama cut transits to 32 a day on 1 September 2026, naming this event. Local prices are where the damage lands. World staple-grain prices did not rise in the strongest past El Niños; the effects that show are small and commodity-specific (vegetable oils, sugar). See Prices.

cascade.what: Emergency caseloads in southern Africa, the Horn and the Dry Corridor.
cascade.note: 2015-16 and 2023-24 both produced regional emergencies of tens of millions within roughly 6–18 months of the ONI peak.

context.caveat: The Cole et al. finding is about the last forty years as a class, not about this event individually, and its own authors frame it as a millennial-context claim. It is here to show that the recent run of strong eastern-Pacific events is itself unusual, which is a separate claim from anything this page says about 2026.

feedback.title: And then it feeds back on itself
feedback.text: They close into a loop. Weaker trades let the warm pool slide east; the warm pool moving east flattens the west-to-east sea-surface temperature gradient; and that gradient is precisely what drives the trades. So the weakening feeds the weakening. This is the Bjerknes feedback, and it is why a small initial nudge can grow into an event of this size rather than simply decaying.
feedback.closes: The loop runs 3 → 1: the warm water that step 1 released is what keeps step 1 going.
feedback.brake: What stops it is not shown here. The loop is eventually broken by slow ocean waves off the equator that return cold water to the eastern Pacific months later, the delayed-oscillator mechanism. That is why El Niño events end rather than running away, and why they tend to peak near the end of the calendar year.

sources.label: Bjerknes, J. (1969), Atmospheric teleconnections from the equatorial Pacific

data.figure_note: Schematic, and vertically exaggerated. The sea-surface tilt is real: the western Pacific stands about half a metre higher than the eastern. Half a metre across 15,000 km would be invisible at this scale, so it is drawn many times steeper than life. Depths are indicative: the thermocline sits roughly 100–200 m down in the west and far shallower in the east. Read the shapes, not the proportions.
